newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Profiles of Indonesian parties in May 29 poll.
newsitem.headline: Profiles of Indonesian parties in May 29 poll.

text.p: Following are profiles of the three political parties legally permitted to contest Indonesia's general election next Thursday for the 425 elected seats in the 500-seat House of Representatives.
The remaining 75 seats are alloted to the military which does not vote.

GOLKAR - Founded in 1964 by a group of soldiers and civilians to offset the pervasive influence of the Communist Party of Indonesia (PKI). The PKI was banned after being blamed for an abortive 1965 coup attempt which led to General Suharto replacing founding President Sukarno as head of state.

Golkar, which stands for "functional groups", has been the dominant party during President Suharto's 30-year rule. It claims a membership of 36 million out of the country's 200 million population. Its general chairman is Information Minister Harmoko, the first civilian to hold the position.

Golkar officials say they have set a target of 70 percent of the 124.7 million voters in the 1997 election compared to 68 percent of the poll in 1992 and 73 percent in 1987. It is the richest party backed by the military, government bureaucracy and leading businessmen.

In its manifesto, Golkar has pushed government programmes ranging from infrastructural, industrial and agricultural development to social welfare through the sprawling archipelago of over 17,000 islands.

UNITED DEVELOPMENT PARTY (PPP) - A Moslem-oriented party, it arose from the merger under government pressure of four Islamic parties in 1973. The PPP is mainly rural-based, with much of its support on the main island of Java.
Officials say they do not have a membership figure.
The PPP is chaired by veteran politician Ismail Hasan Metareum, who campaigned on a theme of "justice" and anti-corruption.
The PPP won 17 percent of the vote and 62 seats in parliament in 1992 compared to a peak of 99 seats in 1977.
Most of the violence during the election campaign period from April 27 to May 23 was between partisans of the PPP and Golkar in Central and West Java.
INDONESIAN DEMOCRATIC PARTY (PDI) - The Christian- Nationalist PDI was also formed under government pressure from several Christian and nationalist parties at the same time as the PPP in 1973.

It has been riven by factional strife since its leader elected for a five-year term in 1993, Megawati Sukarnoputri, was ousted by government-backed rebels headed by deputy parliamentary Speaker Surjadi in June last year.
Megawati, daughter of founding president Sukarno, has been fighting her ouster through the courts.

Electoral authorities refused to accept her candidates' list for the election. She has said she would not vote and told her supporters not to vote for the official PDI candidates, describing the government-backed faction as illegal and unconstitutional. PDI rallies were notably lacklustre during the campaign.
The PDI, which won 15 percent of the vote in 1992, claims a membership of 16 million. Surjadi said its aim was to promote democracy, social justice and the spirit of nationalism.
